newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FUN IN BRUSSELS - LAUGHING AT LAWYERS WITH DAUMIER.
newsitem.headline: FUN IN BRUSSELS - LAUGHING AT LAWYERS WITH DAUMIER.

text.p: The French Cour de Cassation could not possibly have known how timely an exhibition of Honore Daumier lithographs about the court and politics would be in post-Dutroux Belgium, but here it is.

A series of cartoons by the 19th century French master of social satire, first shown at the Paris Cour de Cassation last year, is on view at the Brussels Town Hall just weeks after the Belgian parliament issued its scathing report on bungling by police, the courts and government in the paedophile murder scandal.
In the aftermath of this case, in which Marc Dutroux is the main suspect, Daumier's caustic cartoons about greedy lawyers, sleepy judges and lazy politicians look sharper than ever.

In Daumier's drawings, well-fed judges lean back in their chairs, look down at a poor defendant and say things like: "Hunger, hunger, that is no excuse, I am hungry nearly every day but that does not make me a thief."

But Daumier's favourite targets always were lawyers. In another classic in his "Gens de justice" (People of the Law) collection, an arrogant laywer steps away from a desperate client saying: "My dear sir, it is absolutely impossible for me to plead your case ... some important notes are missing from your file ... (aside) ... 100 franc notes, that is".
Daumier's black-and-white drawings look so modern they could feature in the New Yorker magazine. Equally important are the irreverent captions.
Here are another few samples, freely translated from French:

Lawyer to a sad-looking woman: "True, you've lost your case, but you must have had a good time hearing me plead". A lawyer in a courtroom whispers to his client: "The prosecutor is saying unpleasant things about you, try to cry a little, that always helps."
None of the individual cartoons will crack you up, but the sheer volume of Daumier's output explains his impact on generations of cartoonists after him.

Like the satirical English painter and engraver William Hogarth (1697-1764) before him, Daumier (1808-1879) made a career out of portraying human vice and folly, immortalising the evil side of his fellow Parisiens in more than 3,000 lithographs.

Unfortunately, the Brussels exhibition does not do justice to Daumier's productivity. There are only 26 lithographs (engravings in stone) of "Les Gens de justice", which were first published in the satirical magazine "Le Charivari" between 1845 and 1848.
In a second room, there are cartoons of French 19th century politicians, but these have not stood the test of time so well.

Luckily, the organisors are selling the beautiful 1979 Editions Michele Trinckvel series of books with Daumier cartoons about selected topics, such as Les Gens d'Affaires, Les Gens de Medecine, Les Gens du Spectacle, Locataires et proprietaires, Les Gens de Justice, and Intellectuelles et femmes socialistes.
If you know any brokers, bankers, lawyers, doctors or house owners with a sense of humour, these books, which normaly only occasionaly pop up in antiquarian bookstores, make a wonderful present.

PRACTICAL: Exhibition Justice et Politique - Gerecht en Politiek, Honore Daumier caricatures, Brussels town hall, Grand Place, open 1300 to 1800 Tuesday to Saturday, 1100 to 1700 on Sunday, until June 1. Entrance 150 francs. The books cost 700 francs.
